text.en: Before the work starts, understand the sequence
formwork → reinforcement → embeds/openings → pre-pour → concrete placement → testing → curing → stripping → post-pour inspection
Plan around the actual construction schedule.
Which preceding work must already be accepted?
What future structural steel/equipment interfaces rely on this pour?
Is there temporary shoring/re-shoring that affects the quality sequence?
A dimension error on Level 1 may propagate upward.
grid → elevation → column/wall location → slab edge → embeds → next-level interface
rather than treating each pour in isolation.
A revised electrical equipment room requires a new floor opening.
The old structural drawing does not show it, but an approved technical change does.
If the pour proceeds using the old layout, you may end up saw-cutting structural concrete later.
technical change control before pour is critical.
You should be able to answer
Which concrete went into this exact column/slab/wall, which tests correspond to it, what issues occurred, and how were they resolved?
After stripping a wall, you observe severe honeycombing around a congested reinforcement zone.
Do not assume every honeycombed area is a cosmetic patch.
These trends can reveal process failures upstream.

text.en: Precast panel arrives with corner spall.
Identify member → photograph → determine extent → control installation if necessary → obtain approved repair disposition → repair or replace → reinspect → document → release.
Before considering a structural zone complete
A structural element is not “quality complete” merely because it is physically standing.
correct requirement + approved material + correct installation + required inspection/testing + objective evidence + resolved deviations + verified closure
Absolutely. Building envelope deserves one of the deepest modules in the whole system because envelope defects are often:
difficult to diagnose once the building is closed;
directly tied to water infiltration, air leakage, condensation, heat loss, mold, corrosion, and occupant complaints.

Create a continuous, durable, coordinated environmental separation between exterior and interior conditions, with controlled water, air, vapour and heat flow across walls, openings, penetrations and transitions.
And the key word is continuity.
A wall can have excellent insulation, excellent membrane, excellent flashing, and still fail if those systems are not properly connected at:
windows → doors → roof → foundation → penetrations → corners → joints → structural interfaces.
So our envelope QC system must inspect not only components, but also interfaces.
